title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
hook: the one who wanted proof gets invited to touch the wounds
carry: doubt is allowed in the room

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emmaus, where hearts burned and the stranger was known in the breaking of bread. Today, someone who wasn't convinced.

You've missed something big. The group chat is exploding. Everybody was there except you, and what they're telling you sounds impossible. Back in Jerusalem, there's a locked room. On the evening of that first Sunday, John says, Jesus came and stood among the disciples, said peace be unto you, and showed them his hands and his side. But one of the twelve wasn't there: Thomas, called Didymus, the twin. When the others tell him, we've seen the Lord, he doesn't just nod along.
screen: `EVERYONE WAS THERE BUT YOU.` → `A LOCKED ROOM, A FIRST SUNDAY.` → `THOMAS WASN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: Thomas says, in the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's where doubting Thomas comes from. But look at who he was before. When Jesus decided to go back into Judea, where, his disciples reminded him, people had just tried to stone him, Thomas said: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." And at the last supper, when Jesus spoke about going away, Thomas was honest enough to say, we don't know where you're going; how can we know the way? Read that way, he doesn't look like a skeptic by nature. He's brave, and he asks what others may be thinking. Eight days later they're together again behind shut doors, and Thomas is with them. Jesus stands among them: "Peace be unto you." He goes straight to Thomas, offering exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't throw Thomas out for doubting. He comes back for him. And a surprise: the text never says Thomas touched him, only what he answered: "My Lord and my God." Some readers hear it as one of the fullest confessions of who Jesus is in the Gospels, from the one who doubted. Then Jesus says: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." Tradition says Thomas later carried the news as far as India, and the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.
screen: `EXCEPT I SHALL SEE.` · `LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE.` · `REACH HITHER THY FINGER.` · `THE DOUBTER'S CONFESSION.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of one doubt you carry, about God, faith, something you were taught, or yourself, the kind that's easy to hide, as if having one means not belonging. Say it out loud, gently, in one sentence, not as an attack, just the truth, and notice what happens. If you pray, bring the doubt to God just as it is.
Thomas. Called Didymus, the twin. The one who wanted proof, and who then said: my Lord and my God.
Your line: doubt is allowed in the room. Tomorrow, breakfast on a beach. See you then.

howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Thomas on the Sunday after Easter, which Orthodox Christians call Thomas Sunday. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, in India, trace their church to the apostle, and many churches keep his feast in July or December.

original.note: Greek: twin. John says Thomas was called Didymus; some readers hear the same meaning in the Aramaic name Thomas.

trapdoor: what you thought: doubting Thomas, the one who didn't believe.
what it means: a brave, honest disciple who asked for what the others had already seen, and was met there, not rejected.

what a scholar hears: the text never says he touched the wounds, some readers call his my Lord and my God one of the fullest confessions in the Gospels, and the Thomas Christians of India trace their church to him.

notes: 'The fullest confession of who Jesus is anywhere in the Gospels' is a common scholarly judgment, not settled; reviewer softened teach, word and trapdoor to 'one of the fullest'. Confirm.
Reviewer softened 'Thomas isn't a skeptic by nature' to an interpretive reading ('read that way ... doesn't look like'), since his character is inferred from John 11:16 and 14:5.
The text does not say Thomas touched the wounds; stated plainly. Some traditions and art assume he did.
Thomas in India: tradition of the Saint Thomas Christians (Kerala), with arrival traditionally dated AD 52; stated as tradition.

Feast of Saint Thomas: July 3 (Catholic, Anglican), December 21 (older Western calendar and some Anglican/Lutheran), October 6 (Orthodox); Thomas Sunday is the Sunday after Pascha. howItsDone says 'July or December'; Keeper may add October.
Thomas from Aramaic te'oma, 'twin'; Didymus the Greek. Confirm.
